text: Welcome, curators. Our museum is building a diorama of a Haudenosaunee longhouse. Visit one in VR, then record a short video for me.
No headset today? Come to the collections room. Put each museum card on the timeline. Then tell me what you found.
Have more time? Turn slowly while you record, so I can see both ends of the longhouse.
Before your headset, look at how a longhouse is built. Then press Practice and say your two sentences before the timer ends.
Open the On-Demand app. Click Explore. Type Longhouse in the filter box, click Iroquois Longhouse, then click Begin Solo.
Move with the thumbstick. Look at the walls and the roof. Find one spot where you can see a lot of the longhouse.
Open Library, then Camera. Click Record video and say your two sentences. Click again to stop. Then send it on the Canvas tab.
Press the Meta button and click Quit. Then open the Canvas assignment and check that your video is there.

All four labels are up! Now look at the postcards. Each one is a real photo from our region. Turn each postcard over and read the back. It tells you where the photo was taken. Then pin it on that place on the map.

Last job of the day! Visitors need to know where they are, so you'll write the gallery introduction. First, finish the direction sentence. Tap a direction word for each blank. Then add one sentence of your own. When it's ready, open your gallery!
Finish the direction sentence. Then add one sentence of your own. Then open your gallery.
Look at the space picture first. Then drag the slider to the right to add the map lines.
Read the clue on the label. Then tap the place on the map where it belongs.

Hoo, hello, curator! You finished the World Map Hall. Now a brand-new room is ready: the North America and Caribbean Gallery. To get there, start with the big globe. Turn the globe. Zoom in. And remember our lens today, courtesy. Real people live in every place we study, so we say each name with care.

Welcome to the gallery! The big map on the wall shows one part of the world. Four places on it are waiting for labels. Read the clue on each label. Use the compass rose to find north, south, east, and west. Then tap the place where the label belongs.
Here's a puzzle for you. Canada and the United States are next-door neighbors. Which one is bigger? And which one has more people? Press the buttons one at a time and find out.
This is our region seen from space. NASA made this picture from lots of satellite photos. Look closely at the land first. Then use the slider to add the map lines, and watch what changes.

Here is the label cart. Every label is hidden under a cloth. Lift the cloth on one label. Look at the photo and read the clue. Then tap the drawer it belongs in: mountains, rivers, plains, or islands.

Last job of the day! Our physical map needs a label for visitors. Pick a photo for your label. Then write your label in the Curator Task box. Name a mountain range, a river, and one more feature, and say where each one is. When you're ready, open your exhibit!
Lift the cloth on one label. Look at the photo and read the clue. Then tap the drawer where it belongs.
Pick a photo. Write your label in the Curator Task box above. Then press Open my exhibit.
Do the steps one at a time: tilt the map, cut the slice, then walk across it.

Hoo, hello again, curator! Last time we hung the country labels on the big wall map. Today a cart full of brand-new labels has rolled into the museum. These labels are not for countries. They are for the land itself. And remember our lens, courtesy. Many of today's names, like Mississippi and Appalachian, come from the first peoples who lived here. So we say each name with care.
What happens when rain falls on tall mountains? Make it rain on the Rocky Mountains. Then follow the water and watch where every river goes.
This is a real physical map of our region. A physical map shows the land, not the countries. Use the color key to read it. Then turn on the borders and look closely at the mountains.
Welcome to the relief table! Right now it looks like a flat map. Tilt the map, and watch the land stand up. Then cut a slice across the United States, and walk across it from west to east.
Here's the Exhibit Floor! Visitors will read the label you write. A good label tells what the resource is, where it comes from, how people use it, and one honest limit. You've got this!

Welcome to the Gallery! Our biggest exhibit is the Time-Lapse Case. It is a model with four glass boxes: a forest, two fish tanks, and oil under the ground. First you'll make a guess. Then you'll watch people use the resources. Then you'll drag the time lever to the right to move forward in time. Let's see what happens!
Drag each specimen into the case where it belongs. Or tap a specimen, then tap a case.
Press and hold a crate until the lid pops off. Then do the steps on the desk, one at a time.
Pick one specimen. Then write your label in the Curator Task box. Your words show up under your specimen as you type. When you have twenty words, tap Open my exhibit.

Hoo, hello, curator! Big news. Six crates just came in the back door of our North America and Caribbean Gallery. Inside are things the land gives us, like wood, wheat, water, fish, copper, and oil. Each crate has a tag that says where it came from. But a tag doesn't tell the whole story. Your job today is to find out how people use each one. And be honest about something curators sometimes leave out: not everything the land gives us lasts forever.
All six are in the log! Did you notice? Bread, paper, fish sticks, and gas did not start at a store. They all started on the land. Next, walk through the door to the Gallery. That's room two.
Time to fill the display cases! Every object from the crates goes in one of two cases. Think back to the time lever. Which ones came back?

These are real photos taken long ago, in three different places on the Great Plains. The Great Plains are the wide, flat lands in the middle of our country. Tap each small photo to see it big. Then tap the numbered dots to learn what you're looking at.

Here's a little experiment. Two trays hold the same soil. Tray 1 has bare soil. Tray 2 has grass growing in it. A fan will blow the same wind on both. First, make a guess. Which tray will keep more of its soil?
This is the Workroom, where curators check their notes before they build an exhibit. Answer one question at a time. If you miss one, read why, and keep going. That's how curators learn.
